definition: Quixotic means idealistic in an impractical, unrealistic way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word quixotic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know quixotic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everyone loves Grandpa Milo's quixotic pledge to translate the town's entire archive into Esperanto; the archive gains a shelf a week, and Grandpa is eighty-one.
Hopeful is the mild, grounded end — expecting things may go well — far short of quixotic, which mounts a campaign the arithmetic has already condemned.
Starry-eyed dreamers ignore the odds, but they stop short of quixotic: the quixotic go one step past dreaming and actually ride at the windmill.

Utopian dreams a perfected world on paper — ideal societies, flawless systems, no rough edges. Quixotic shares the idealism but saddles up and charges at the real world, odds and all. The utopian writes the blueprint; the quixotic soul rides at the actual windmill with whatever is in the shed.

Impractical means it won't work, plainly stated — a verdict with no affection in it. Quixotic delivers the same verdict while smiling: the plan is doomed and noble at once, romantic in its doomedness. Call a filing system impractical; save quixotic for doomed crusades you half admire.
sizes up the odds and plans inside them
unmoved by romance; runs on evidence and arithmetic

There is no root to reuse — the word is one man's name with -ic bolted on. Don Quixote is fiction's most famous impractical idealist, and English simply turned him into an adjective. (Note the pronunciation while you're here: the knight is 'kee-HOH-tay,' but the adjective is plain English 'kwik-SOT-ik.')
Quixotic means idealistic in an impractical, unrealistic way.
His quixotic project to reunite every lost glove in the city — he kept a warehouse of left hands waiting for their partners — charmed the newspapers and emptied his savings account twice.

Quixotic is more precise than 'unrealistic' because it adds nobility and romance to the doomed arithmetic: a quixotic plan charges at something huge and worthy with equipment that cannot possibly win.
We smile at quixotic people even while wincing at their budgets.
Quixotic smiles while it doubts: use it for noble long shots you half admire — a one-boat cleanup, a solo reforestation.
'Impractical' is the same verdict without the affection.
Its unit-mate fatalistic is its mirror opposite: the fatalist has ruled that effort changes nothing, while the quixotic soul stakes everything on effort the numbers have already vetoed.

The Milford canal has been silted shut since 1931, which is precisely why Arthur Penn is building a boat for it.
Every town meeting hears the same numbers: dredging would cost eleven million dollars the town does not have, and no cargo has wanted a canal since the railroad came.
Arthur nods along and keeps building; neighbors call the project quixotic, and most of them mean it fondly.
He knows the odds better than anyone, having compiled them for the council himself.
But he believes a town should be able to see one beautiful, doomed argument for its own history, planked and varnished, waiting for water that may never come.
